abstract: The medial prefrontal cortex (mPFC) displays a delayed maturation long hypothesized to guide developmental changes in threat processing. Nevertheless, the mechanism by which ontogenetic changes in mPFC function guide the developmental emergence of behavior is unclear. Early life marks a shift between a permanent extinction phenotype typical of juveniles, toward the standard, more transient extinction seen in adult rodents. This shift coincides with developmental changes in mPFC-amygdala connectivity, a pathway necessary for extinction processing in adults. Here we used optogenetics and slice electrophysiology to show that, in contrast to adult animals, juvenile mice displaying permanent extinction fail to engage the mPFC-amygdala pathway at the synaptic, cell activity or behavioral levels. Consistent with a requirement of this pathway for the developmental transition in extinction types, optic potentiation of the mPFC-amygdala pathway accelerates the onset of adult extinction. Our findings show that the developmental onboarding of the mPFC-amygdala pathway drives a shift in extinction processing toward increased fear reemergence that persists throughout adulthood.
